rationale: C25 plausibly supplied a compact rhetorical template that the child adapted from prisoners and populations behind the Iron Curtain to the people of Czechoslovakia: millions living under communism have lost freedom and dignity, look to the free world for hope, and should be encouraged to endure. C16 contains a closely related but broader sequence concerning human dignity, totalitarian enslavement, religious repression, and free-world solidarity. C23 also parallels the child's emphasis on communicating truth behind the Iron Curtain, but its concrete subject is an information-program appropriation rather than an anniversary message.

shared_material.child_excerpt: The dark night of communist enslavement, bringing the loss of freedom, civil rights and human dignity... now unhappily covers your land.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: behind the Iron Curtain there are millions of people who yearn desperately to regain their lost freedom and sense of dignity.
shared_material.explanation: Both use the paired loss of freedom and human dignity to characterize populations under communist rule.

shared_material.child_excerpt: the Government and people of the United States and all free countries look upon the present plight of the people of Czechoslovakia... so that they may take heart and remain firm
shared_material.parent_excerpt: These people look to the free world as their only hope to achieve this goal.
shared_material.explanation: The child adapts C25's free-world-as-hope construction into a message of encouragement and solidarity.

shared_material.child_excerpt: the suffering millions in your homeland who are faithful disciples of democracy
shared_material.parent_excerpt: behind the Iron Curtain there are millions of people who yearn desperately to regain their lost freedom
shared_material.explanation: The shared focus on millions subjected to communist government and longing for restored freedom is concrete and central to both letters.
